lead: A language processor is software that reads a program written in one language and prepares it to run or runs it. A translator converts source text into another form. A compiler translates the whole source into a target program, usually machine code, before any run. An interpreter reads and executes source or intermediate code statement by statement, so its output is the running result. An assembler translates assembly mnemonics into machine instructions, usually one mnemonic to one instruction. These tools exist because humans write in C, Python or assembly, while the processor executes only its own instruction set.

blocks.text: A language processor is any program that takes a source program and turns it into a form that can execute, or executes it. A translator is a language processor that rewrites the source into another language. A compiler is a translator: it reads the complete source, checks it, and emits a target program. In a C workflow, the compiler produces machine code; the user runs that code later, many times if needed. A assembler is also a translator, but it works at a lower level: it maps assembly mnemonics such as MOV and ADD to machine instructions, usually one-to-one. An interpreter is different. It does not hand the user a target program. It reads the source or an intermediate form and performs the actions of each statement as it goes; the output appears during interpretation. Python commonly works this way: the Python system executes your file and prints results, rather than leaving a standalone machine-code file for you to run. Hybrid systems exist. Java compiles source to bytecode, and a virtual machine interprets that bytecode or compiles it further just in time. The central question is timing: does translation finish before execution, or does execution drive translation?

The output tells you which tool you are looking at. A compiler's output is a target program: an executable, an object file, or assembly text, depending on the compiler. An interpreter's output is the result of the program: values printed, files changed, a service started. An assembler's output is object code: machine instructions plus information the linker needs. The same source can be handled either way. C is normally compiled. Python is normally interpreted, with internal compilation to bytecode first. Assembly is assembled, then linked with other object files to form an executable. Compile-then-run favours repeated runs: you pay translation once, then run a fast target program. Interpret-as-you-go favours quick starts and portability: no separate machine-code file is needed, and the interpreter can run wherever it is installed. The price is repeated work on every run, because the interpreter must examine statements again. The worked example below turns this trade-off into arithmetic.

A compiler rarely works alone. Around it sit other language processors, often called the cousins of the compiler; some syllabi call the whole group a language processing system. A preprocessor prepares source before compilation. In C it handles #include, #define and conditional compilation. A macro processor replaces macro calls by their defined bodies; it is a general text-substitution tool, while the C preprocessor is a specialised one. A linker joins object files and library code into one executable, resolving names that one file uses and another defines. A loader places that executable in memory and starts it, setting up addresses at load time. A compiler may also call an assembler to turn its assembly output into object code. These tools matter because real builds chain them: source → preprocessor → compiler → assembler → linker → loader → running process. The compiler is the central translator, not the whole factory.

figure.caption: Cost in seconds for r runs from the worked example: the interpreter costs 3 s every run, while the compiler costs 4 s once and then 0.10 s per run. The lines cross before run 2, so at 2 runs the compiled cost is 4.2 s against the interpreted 6 s.

examples.question: A program has 100 statements. An interpreter costs 0.03 s per statement on every run. A compiler costs 4 s once, and the compiled code costs 0.10 s per run. Find the smallest number of runs after which compiling is cheaper.
steps: Interpreted cost per run = 100 × 0.03 s = 3 s.
Compiled cost for r runs = 4 + 0.10r seconds. Here 4 s is the one-time compile cost and 0.10 s is the per-run code cost.
r is a whole number of runs, so the smallest r is 2.
Check r = 2: compiled cost = 4 + 0.10×2 = 4.2 s; interpreted cost = 3×2 = 6 s. At r = 1, compiled cost = 4.1 s and interpreted cost = 3 s, so compiling is not cheaper.
examples.answer: The smallest number is 2 runs; at 2 runs the compiled cost is 4.2 s and the interpreted cost is 6 s.
examples.check:
import math
statements = 100
interp_per_stmt = 0.03
compile_once = 4.0
compiled_per_run = 0.10
interp_per_run = statements * interp_per_stmt
gap = interp_per_run - compiled_per_run
threshold = compile_once / gap
r = math.ceil(threshold)
compiled_total = compile_once + compiled_per_run * r
interp_total = interp_per_run * r
print(interp_per_run)
print(round(gap, 2))
print(round(threshold, 3))
print(r)
print(round(compiled_total, 1))
print(round(interp_total, 1))

traps: Both a compiler and an interpreter translate, so the difference is when. A compiler produces a target program before execution; an interpreter executes source or intermediate code during the run.
An assembler is not a compiler. It maps assembly mnemonics to machine instructions, usually one-to-one; a compiler translates a high-level language and may emit many instructions per statement.
Do not say an interpreter produces machine code for later runs. Its output is the result of execution. Hybrid bytecode systems blur the boundary, but the interpreter still executes.
In break-even problems, compile cost is once and run cost is per run. Set one-time cost + per-run compiled cost < per-run interpreted cost, and round up because runs are whole.

quiz.a: A language processor reads a source program and prepares it to run or runs it. A translator rewrites source text into another language.

quiz.q: Why can an interpreter start faster than a compiler but cost more on many runs?
quiz.a: It starts executing without making a full target program. On every run it must examine and execute statements again, so repeated runs pay the interpretation cost each time.

quiz.q: A program has 50 statements. An interpreter costs 0.04 s per statement per run. A compiler costs 3 s once and compiled code costs 0.20 s per run. Find the smallest number of runs after which compiling is cheaper.
quiz.a: Interpreted cost per run = 50 × 0.04 = 2 s. Compiled cost = 3 + 0.20r. Solve 3 + 0.20r < 2r → 3 < 1.80r → r > 1.667. Smallest integer r = 2. Check: compiled 3.4 s, interpreted 4 s.

quiz.q: A student says Python is not compiled because it uses an interpreter. Is that complete?
quiz.a: No. Python usually compiles source to bytecode first, then a virtual machine interprets the bytecode. It is a hybrid model, not pure source interpretation.

quiz.q: Name four cousins of the compiler and one job each.
quiz.a: Preprocessor prepares source; macro processor expands macros; linker joins object files and libraries; loader places the executable in memory and starts it.

quiz.q: What is the output of a compiler, an interpreter and an assembler?
quiz.a: Compiler: a target program. Interpreter: the result of the running program. Assembler: object code.

quiz.q: Why is an assembler's translation usually one-to-one while a compiler's is not?
quiz.a: Assembly mnemonics correspond closely to machine instructions, so one mnemonic usually maps to one instruction. A high-level statement such as an assignment can need many machine instructions, so a compiler translates one statement into a sequence.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real systems mix these models: Java virtual machines, JavaScript engines and Python runtimes use bytecode plus just-in-time compilation. WebAssembly gives a portable target that browsers compile or interpret. LLVM separates a language front end from target code generation, so many languages share optimisers and back ends. Search next for just-in-time compilation, bytecode, LLVM IR and WebAssembly.
